text:
The passage rewards a reader who attends to what is missing from it. Sarah appears nowhere in the chapter, and the book announces her death in the verse immediately following; the scene implies, without ever stating, that something in the household did not survive the mountain. Abraham returns to the servants, and Isaac is not mentioned. The narrator turns away at the very moment a lesser story would linger, and the silence is itself a kind of testimony.

It may be objected that the chapter merely follows the conventions of ancient narrative, which rarely reports feeling and never explains. There is perhaps some truth in this. But the narrator elsewhere tells what characters feel: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The reticence here is deliberate, and the narrator knows what he is about. Restraint, in such a voice, becomes a kind of accusation.
